--- title: "Linear Regression" jupyter: python3 format: revealjs: scrollable: true navigation-mode: vertical controls-layout: bottom-right controls-tutorial: true incremental: false theme: [default, styles.scss] revealjs-plugins: - pointer - verticator filters: - code-fullscreen - reveal-auto-agenda editor: source order: 4 --- ## Learning Objectives - Fit and interpret a simple linear regression model with the formula API - Add continuous and categorical predictors to a regression model - Fit the same models from design matrices with the matrix API ## Python Modules, Functions, and Parameters ::: {#344f4133 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm import statsmodels.formula.api as smf from plotnine import * from plotnine.data import penguins as penguins_data ``` ::: ## Scatter Plot ::: {#a8c1edc1 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29} ![](3a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){width=960 height=480} ::: ::: ## Data Prep ::: {#513caf62 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins = ( penguins_data .copy() .dropna() ) ``` ::: # Linear Regression ## Linear Regression Linear regression is used to model the association between a set of predictor variables (x's) and an outcome variable (y). Linear regression will fit a line that best describes the data points. ## Scatter Plot ::: {#663818b2 .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=31} ![](3a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=960 height=480} ::: ::: ## Simple Linear Regression Simple linear regression will model the association between one predictor variable and an outcome: $$ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \epsilon $$ - $\beta_0$: Intercept term - $\beta_1$: Slope term - $\epsilon\sim N(0,\sigma^2)$ ## Estimated Model $$ \hat Y = \hat \beta_0 + \hat \beta_1 X $$ ## Process ![](img/6b1.gif){fig-align="center"} ## Process ::: {#5dd4c3c2 .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=32} ![](3a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-7-output-1.png){width=960 height=480} ::: ::: ## Sums of Error Squared $$ RSS = \sum^n_{i=1}(Y_i-\hat Y_i)^2 $$ ## Searching ::: {#7276f137 .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=33} ![](3a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-8-output-1.png){width=960 height=480} ::: ::: ## Searching ::: {#68909769 .cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=34} ![](3a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-9-output-1.png){width=960 height=480} ::: ::: ## Searching ::: {#21bac2f0 .cell execution_count=9} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=35} ![](3a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-10-output-1.png){width=960 height=480} ::: ::: ## Searching ::: {#1d915dc2 .cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=36} ![](3a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-11-output-1.png){width=960 height=480} ::: ::: ## Final ::: {#3a34fa19 .cell execution_count=11} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=37} ![](3a_files/figure-revealjs/cell-12-output-1.png){width=960 height=480} ::: ::: # Python Code ## Model Syntax The `statsmodels.formula.api` module lets us describe a regression model with a formula: ::: {#8ad617be .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} # outcome ~ predictor model = smf.ols( "Y ~ X", data=DATA ).fit() ``` ::: - The variable `Y` to the left of `~` is the outcome - Variable `X` to the right of `~` are predictors - `DATA` is the name of the pandas data frame - `.fit()` estimates the regression coefficients ## Penguins Example Data The fitted equation is $$ \widehat{\text{body mass}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1(\text{flipper_length}). $$ The slope estimates the change in mean body mass associated with a one-millimeter increase in flipper length. ## Fitting Model ::: {#430ab48d .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} model_1 = smf.ols( "body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm", data=penguins ).fit() ``` ::: ## Examming Output ::: {#e860c12f .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Coefficient table with standard errors, test statistics, # p-values, and confidence intervals model_1.summary().tables[1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=39} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Predict Body Mass Prediction data must use the same predictor name as the model formula. ::: {#d0e159ac .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} new_penguins = pd.DataFrame( {"flipper_length_mm": [190, 200, 210]} ) penguins_pred = model_1.get_prediction( new_penguins ).summary_frame() penguins_pred ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=40} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: # Multivariable Linear Regression ## MLR Multivariable linear regression models are used when more than one explanatory variable is used to explain the outcome of interest. ## Continuous Variable Add predictors on the right side of the formula with `+`: $$Y = \beta_0 +\beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2$$ ::: {#3340bd67 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} model = smf.ols( "Y ~ X1 + X2", data=DATA, ).fit() ``` ::: - The variable `Y` is the outcome - Variables `X1` and `X2` are the predictors - `DATA` is the name of the pandas data frame - `.fit()` estimates the regression coefficients ## Example Using the Palmer Penguins data, fit a model with `body_mass_g` as the outcome and `flipper_length_mm` and `bill_length_mm` as predictors. ::: {#4866b39f .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} model_2 = smf.ols( "body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + bill_length_mm", data=penguins, ).fit() model_2.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=41} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Categorical Variable A categorical variable can be included in a model, but a reference category must be specified. ## Fitting a model with categorical variables To fit a model with categorical variables, we must utilize dummy (binary) variables that indicate which category is being referenced. We use $C-1$ dummy variables where $C$ indicates the number of categories. When coded correctly, each category will be represented by a combination of dummy variables. ## Example If we have 4 categories, we will need 3 dummy variables: | | Cat 1 | Cat 2 | Cat 3 | Cat 4 | |---------|-------|-------|-------|-------| | Dummy 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | | Dummy 2 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | | Dummy 3 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | Which one is the reference category? ## Fitting a model with categorical variables ::: {#985db36e .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} model = smf.ols( "Y ~ X1 + C(X2)", data=DATA, ).fit() ``` ::: - The variable `Y` is the outcome - `X1` is a nemerical predictor - `X2` is a categorical predictor variable - `DATA` is the name of the pandas data frame - `.fit()` estimates the regression coefficients ## Island Variable ::: {#262f543f .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( penguins["island"] .value_counts() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=43} ``` island Biscoe 163 Dream 123 Torgersen 47 Name: count, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ## Fitting a model with categorical variables Using the Palmer Penguins data, fit a model with `body_mass_g` as the outcome and `flipper_length_mm` and `island` as predictors. ::: {#3446189c .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} model_3 = smf.ols( "body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + " "C(island)", data=penguins, ).fit() model_3.summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=44} ```{=html}

Internally, the model creates $C-1$ indicator columns. ::: {#b50bc589 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} model_3.model.exog_names ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=45} ``` ['Intercept', 'C(island)[T.Dream]', 'C(island)[T.Torgersen]', 'flipper_length_mm'] ``` ::: ::: We usually do not create those indicator variables ourselves when using `statsmodels.formula.api`. # Matrix Formulation ## Matrix Formulation $$Y_i = \boldsymbol X_i^\mathrm T \boldsymbol \beta + \epsilon_i$$ - $Y_i$: Outcome Variable - $\boldsymbol X_i$: Predictors - $\boldsymbol \beta$: Coefficients - $\epsilon_i$: error term ## Matrix Formulation $$\boldsymbol\beta = (\boldsymbol X^\mathrm T \boldsymbol X)^{-1} \boldsymbol X^\mathrm T \boldsymbol Y$$ ## Matrix API: Supply $Y$ and $X$ With `statsmodels.api`, we provide the outcome vector and design matrix separately. ::: {#6fb5a260 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} y_matrix = penguins["body_mass_g"] X_matrix = penguins[["flipper_length_mm"]] # statsmodels.api does not add an intercept automatically X_matrix = sm.add_constant(X_matrix) matrix_model = sm.OLS(y_matrix, X_matrix).fit() ``` ::: ## Inspect the Design Matrix Each row represents one penguin, and each column represents one model coefficient. ::: {#3dfb303d .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} X_matrix.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=47} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Multiple Continuous Predictors as a Matrix ::: {#4f4724c5 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} y_continuous = penguins["body_mass_g"] X_continuous = penguins[ ["flipper_length_mm", "bill_length_mm"] ] X_continuous = sm.add_constant(X_continuous) continuous_matrix_model = sm.OLS( y_continuous, X_continuous ).fit() continuous_matrix_model.params.rename( "estimate" ).to_frame() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=50} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Create Indicator Columns for a Category The matrix API requires us to create the indicator columns, we will use `pd.get_dummies` to create them. `drop_first=True` leaves Biscoe as the reference category. ::: {#f521dfd9 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} X_categorical = pd.get_dummies( penguins[ ["flipper_length_mm", "island"] ], columns=["island"], drop_first=True, dtype=float, ) X_categorical = sm.add_constant(X_categorical) X_categorical.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=51} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: The coefficients match the formula model; only the indicator-column names differ. ## Formula API or Matrix API? | Approach | Model specification | Categorical variables | Intercept | |---|---|---|---| | `statsmodels.formula.api` | Formula such as `y ~ x1 + C(group)` | Created automatically | Added automatically | | `statsmodels.api` | Separate `y` vector and `X` matrix | Create indicator columns | Add with `sm.add_constant()` | Use the formula API for readable statistical models. Use the matrix API when you need direct control over the design matrix.
